target_subject: a central figure surrounded by eight other stylized human faces

scene: A black-and-white ink drawing with heavy crosshatching and bold outlines, enclosed within an irregular oval border.
Nine distinct human heads are densely packed; one large head dominates the foreground, while eight smaller heads cluster behind and around it.
All figures exhibit exaggerated facial features—large eyes, distorted noses, and varied expressions—including some wearing round spectacles.

Multiple surrounding figures gaze toward the central figure, with eyes directed inward and mouths slightly open or smiling.
No figure is shown holding a hand near its mouth; all hands are not visible or not engaged in such an action.
rationale: The central figure’s oversized head and forward placement suggest visual hierarchy, though no explicit narrative context confirms dominance.
The uniform monochrome medium and sketchy texture indicate intentional stylistic choice rather than photographic realism.
Facial distortions (e.g., elongated noses, mismatched eye sizes) imply caricature or expressive abstraction, not anatomical accuracy.
object: The central figure has a large circular left eye, a small right eye partially obscured, a prominent ear, and a long curved nose ending in a dark dot.
Eight surrounding heads are individually distinguishable by hairline, eyewear, facial shape, or expression; none share identical features.
Two of the surrounding figures wear round-framed spectacles: one in upper center-right and one in lower right.
The figure at lower left has a wide-open mouth, visible teeth, and a sharply pointed nose; shading suggests depth but no background detail.
The oval boundary is uneven and hand-drawn, with thicker line weight at top and thinner at bottom, enclosing all figures without overlap beyond its edge.

surrounding faces as audience or collective perception

limitations: No textual labels or contextual cues confirm intended symbolism; facial expressions are ambiguous and non-normative.

limitations: Eye differences could stem from drawing technique rather than deliberate semiotic variation.

frame as boundary of shared discourse
